citation: Cossio, S., Chiappinotto, S., Dentice, S., Moreal, C., Magro, G., Dussi, G., Palese, A., & Galazzi, A. (2025). Cybersickness and discomfort from head-mounted displays delivering fully immersive virtual reality: A systematic review. Nurse Education in Practice, 85, 104376. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nepr.2025.104376
thesis: A PRISMA/PROSPERO-registered systematic review of 25 studies (2013-2024) on cybersickness and physical discomfort from HMD-delivered fully immersive VR in education, arguing these adverse physiological effects have been historically under-measured as secondary outcomes relative to learning-effectiveness measures; the aggregate evidence is genuinely mixed (roughly half the studies report inconsistent/low cybersickness, a minority report high scores) rather than uniformly alarming, but the review nonetheless concludes educators bear a disclosure, attribution, and documentation duty toward learners, distinct from the boredom/stress produced by disengaging conventional pedagogy.

sections.title: Introduction / Background
sections.summary: Frames VR-HMD growth in education against neglect of side effects as secondary outcomes; distinguishes simulator sickness (SSQ), motion sickness (MSAQ, FMS), cybersickness (VRSQ) terminology and instruments; separates discomfort as an ergonomic construct (weight, pressure, thermal regulation) independent of VR content.

sections.title: Methods
sections.summary: PROSPERO-registered (CRD42024583656) PRISMA systematic review; PICO framework (P = healthy/non-healthy populations all ages; I = fully immersive HMD VR for education; C = other VR modalities or traditional simulation; O = cybersickness/discomfort). CINAHL, Cochrane, PubMed, Scopus searched 2013-2024, English/Italian. JBI checklists for RCT and quasi-experimental appraisal; two independent reviewers plus a third arbiter.

sections.title: Results - Study characteristics and quality
sections.summary: 5,423 records screened (Rayyan) -> 25 included after de-duplication and title/abstract/full-text exclusion. 16 quasi-experimental (64%), 9 RCTs (36%); mostly single-group design (60%); N=3-133; ages 12-74; 72% students/recent graduates, 16% healthcare professionals, 12% non-healthcare. Moderate methodological quality overall, higher among RCTs.

sections.title: Results - Educational content
sections.summary: 21/25 (84%) in health-education settings; HTC Vive (9 studies) and Oculus Quest (7) most-used HMDs; interventions were technical simulation (64%) or 360-degree educational video (36%); exposure 3-74 minutes, 80% stationary.

sections.title: Results - Outcome metrics and timing
sections.summary: Ad hoc questionnaires dominant (52%), simplified SSQ variants (24%), MSAQ/FMS/SSQ-F/VRSQ/VRSQ-G each used once or twice. 52% of studies had a comparison arm but only 28% administered the tool to that comparison group as well.

sections.title: Results - Outcome data
sections.summary: Cybersickness assessed in 24/25 studies; 12/25 inconsistent/very-low scores, 5/25 high scores. Oculomotor disturbances most-reported (9 studies), nausea second (4), disorientation moderate/high in 3. Discomfort assessed in 8 studies (5 minimal, 3 moderate/high), tracking device weight/heat more than exposure duration. Majority pattern: worse cybersickness for HMD vs. desktop/non-immersive VR/traditional sim, with an explicit counter-case (Huber et al. 2018: AR worse than IVR).

sections.title: Discussion
sections.summary: Subsections on study characteristics/quality, educational content, outcome metrics/timing, outcome data, and limitations. Flags instrument heterogeneity, SSQ's flight-simulator origin as a poor fit for HMD VR, under-explored professional/older/patient populations, sex-based susceptibility differences, and the value of delayed post-exposure symptom tracking.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Acknowledges possible selection bias despite protocol registration and PRISMA adherence; notes researchers' educational/clinical disciplinary background may have shaped interpretation; calls for multidisciplinary quality appraisal in future reviews.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.summary: Contrasts VR-HMD's distinct, variable-prevalence physiological symptom profile (oculomotor > nausea > disorientation > discomfort) against the boredom/stress produced by non-engaging conventional pedagogy; argues educators must recognize, attribute, document, and disclose adverse effects (especially where post-session driving is involved) and encourage learner self-report.

constructs.label: cybersickness & physical discomfort
constructs.treatment: Primary, deeply elaborated construct. Disentangles four overlapping terms/instruments: simulator sickness (SSQ, flight-simulator origin, Kennedy et al. 1993), motion sickness (MSAQ, Gianaros et al. 2001; FMS, Keshavarz & Hecht 2011), cybersickness proper (visual/vestibular/proprioceptive sensory mismatch, McCauley & Sharkey 1992; LaViola 2000; measured by VRSQ, Kim et al. 2018), and discomfort as a separate ergonomic construct (device weight, pressure, thermal regulation; Rupp 2024) independent of VR content. Aggregate findings: 12/25 studies inconsistent/very-low cybersickness, 5/25 high; oculomotor disturbances most-reported; discomfort minimal in 5/8 assessing studies.

constructs.label: immersion (technological)
constructs.treatment: Framing construct, not independently tested by the review itself. Adopts a non-/semi-/fully-immersive taxonomy (Martirosov et al. 2022); treats greater immersion as the presumed mechanism for greater sensory conflict and hence worse cybersickness, a causal claim inherited from the aggregated primary literature rather than demonstrated by the review's own design.

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: Definitional gesture only ('sensation of being there'); never operationalized as a measured outcome anywhere in results or discussion.

conditions.label: review / meta-analytic aggregate
conditions.treatment: The review's own design: PRISMA-2020-compliant systematic review, PROSPERO-registered (CRD42024583656), PICO framework, four databases (CINAHL, Cochrane, PubMed, Scopus), 2013-2024, English/Italian; JBI quality appraisal; 5,423 records screened to 25 included studies.

conditions.label: IVR (HMD)
conditions.treatment: The aggregated intervention across all 25 included studies: fully immersive VR via head-mounted display. 16 quasi-experimental/9 RCT; N=3-133; 21/25 in health-education settings; HTC Vive/Oculus Quest most-used; technical-simulation or 360-degree-video interventions; exposure 3-74 min, 80% stationary.

conditions.label: desktop-3D / non-immersive VR
conditions.treatment: Comparator arm in 5/25 studies (e.g. Al-Khiami et al. 2023, three-arm design vs. 2D drawings and desktop VR; Darnall et al. 2020). Cybersickness reported significantly higher for HMD than the non-immersive comparator in 2 of these.

conditions.label: conventional instruction (control)
conditions.treatment: Traditional simulation with mannequins or theory session, comparator in 3/25 studies (Andersen et al. 2023; Babaita et al. 2024; Pedram et al. 2024). HMD reported worse cybersickness than this control in Andersen et al. 2023 and (mixed-reality-mannequin variant) Elsenbast et al. 2024.

readings.claim: Cybersickness, simulator sickness, motion sickness, and VR sickness are overlapping but distinct terms with distinct historical origins and instruments (SSQ from flight simulation; MSAQ/FMS for general motion sickness; VRSQ purpose-built for VR).
Discomfort is a separate ergonomic construct (device weight, pressure, thermal regulation, restricted head mobility) that can occur regardless of VR content.

Cybersickness findings across the 25 included studies are genuinely mixed: 12/25 inconsistent/very-low scores, 5/25 high scores; oculomotor disturbances are the most-reported symptom, followed by nausea and disorientation.
Discomfort, assessed in 8/25 studies, is mostly minimal and tracks device weight/heat more closely than exposure duration.

Worse cybersickness for HMD VR versus desktop displays, non-immersive VR, and traditional simulation was the majority pattern across comparison studies, attributed to greater sensory conflict from higher immersion.
Huber et al. (2018) found cybersickness less prevalent in fully immersive VR (3.3%) than in augmented reality (6.6%), qualifying the majority pattern.

Instrument heterogeneity, and reliance on the SSQ (designed for seated, non-stereoscopic flight simulators) rather than the purpose-built but rarely-used VRSQ, impede cross-study comparability of cybersickness findings.

Female participants and older learners may show greater cybersickness susceptibility (hormonal factors, interpupillary distance, vestibular/cognitive age-related change), though explanatory mechanisms remain unsettled.

Educators deploying HMD VR must recognize, attribute, and document adverse effects and disclose their possibility to learners, especially before post-session activities like driving, and should encourage learner self-report.

tensions.axis: worse-for-HMD majority pattern vs. Huber et al.'s AR-worse-than-IVR counter-case
tensions.note: The review's own aggregate reports HMD VR as generally worse than desktop/non-immersive comparators, but explicitly reports one study (Huber et al. 2018) finding the reverse ordering against augmented reality, which the review does not resolve.

tensions.axis: cybersickness as inconsistent/low in most studies vs. a real minority-high-symptom subset
tensions.note: 12/25 studies report inconsistent/low cybersickness while 5/25 report high scores; the review's own conclusion leans toward taking the phenomenon seriously (disclosure duty) without claiming the aggregate evidence shows a uniformly large effect — the precise stance this cluster's Debate Axis 7 must preserve.

tensions.axis: instrument heterogeneity vs. comparability of findings
tensions.note: Ad hoc questionnaires dominate (52%) over validated scales, and even validated scales (chiefly SSQ) were designed for a different apparatus (flight simulators) than HMD VR; the review argues this undermines cross-study synthesis even as it performs that synthesis.
